To confirm or refute revoked Gmail consent, inspect the failed execution and token-refresh path for provider auth errors such as invalid_grant, access_denied, token revoked, or explicit consent revocation during refresh/send.

Check whether failures are isolated to one tenant/account or present across multiple accounts using the same Gmail provider path; tenant isolation would favor quota/account limits over a broad provider outage.
If rate limiting is confirmed, propose honoring Retry-After, reducing concurrency, and suppressing blind retries that could worsen quota pressure.

notes: Most useful fields to request from the reporter or platform are: exact failure timestamp with timezone; workspace/project/tenant; execution ID or request ID; Gmail account email or stable provider subject; connection ID; operation name; HTTP status; provider error code/message/reason; refresh-token outcome; granted scopes; last successful send time; retry count; queue/dispatch timestamps; and raw provider response body if captured.

How to distinguish common causes with logs/queries: expired credentials or revoked consent -> refresh/send 401 or invalid_grant/access_denied plus stale last_refresh_success_at; missing scope/permission -> 403 insufficientPermissions/notAuthorized with scope list mismatch; wrong connected account -> connected identity differs from intended sender; rate limit -> 429 or quotaExceeded/userRateLimitExceeded with Retry-After and rising retry volume; provider failure -> upstream 5xx/timeouts after dispatch across multiple tenants; configuration/project mismatch -> execution uses different connection/project/account than intended.

Best first query set once identifiers exist: 1) execution history filtered by time window plus Gmail send operation, 2) canonical logs for the same execution ID, 3) connection/auth records for the referenced connection, 4) metrics comparing failure rate and latency to last healthy period, 5) cross-tenant Gmail error search for the same window.
Because the current dataset has no canonical records, these are triage hypotheses and data requests, not confirmed causes or confirmed healthy checks.

Current evidence is insufficient for a grounded root-cause ranking. The only observed facts are that the user reported Gmail sending stopped and all available queries were partial with no returned canonical records; partial empty queries cannot confirm health or absence of failures.

To narrow common Gmail send failures, collect at least one failed attempt with these identifiers: exact timestamp with timezone, workspace/project/tenant, execution ID or request ID, connection ID, Gmail account email or stable provider subject, operation name, and last known successful send timestamp.

Most discriminating execution-log fields: pipeline stage reached (accepted/queued/auth refresh/dispatched/provider response), internal error class, provider HTTP status, provider error.code, provider error.reason, provider error.message, retry count, queue wait time, provider round-trip latency, and whether a raw provider response body was captured.

Fields that confirm or refute expired credentials or revoked consent: refresh attempt result, refresh error string, refresh HTTP status, token expiry time, last_refresh_success_at, grant status, reconnect history, and provider auth errors such as invalid_grant, unauthorized_client, access_denied, revoked token, or similar 401/403 auth failures.

Fields that confirm or refute missing scope or permission issues: granted scope list, required scope list for the send operation, provider 403 details such as insufficientPermissions or notAuthorized, sender identity used, delegated send-as alias used, and any workspace/admin policy error text.

Fields that confirm or refute wrong account or configuration issues: resolved connection ID, resolved connected account identity, project/workspace ID used by the execution, sender/from address requested, provider subject/email returned by the connection, and whether the execution referenced a different connection than the intended mailbox.

Fields that confirm or refute rate limiting: provider HTTP 429, Google quotaExceeded / userRateLimitExceeded / rateLimitExceeded reasons, Retry-After header, request volume, concurrency, retry amplification, queue backlog, and whether failures correlate with increased send rate.

Fields that confirm or refute provider-side failures: evidence that the request was actually dispatched to Gmail, upstream 5xx or timeout responses, transport/gateway errors after dispatch, latency spikes in provider round-trip, and concurrent similar upstream failures across other tenants/accounts in the same window.

Best next queries once one failed execution or time window is known: (1) execution history for Gmail send attempts in that window, (2) canonical logs for the same execution/request IDs, (3) auth/refresh records for the referenced connection, (4) metrics comparing failure rate/latency/retries/backlog to the last healthy period, and (5) cross-tenant search for Gmail upstream 5xx/429/auth failures in the same interval.

Simple decision rules: if failure occurs before dispatch with refresh/auth errors, favor credential or consent causes; if dispatch occurs and provider returns 403, favor permission/scope/workspace policy; if provider returns 429 with quota reasons, favor provider_rate_limit; if dispatch occurs and multiple tenants show 5xx/timeouts, favor provider_failure; if identity/project/connection do not match the intended mailbox, favor wrong_connected_account or project/configuration mismatch.

Without those records, any diagnosis remains speculative. The fastest useful customer follow-up is: send one exact failed timestamp, the Gmail account involved, any visible error text/code, and either a request/execution ID or a log excerpt around the failure.

recommended_actions: Collect one concrete failed send example: exact timestamp with timezone, workspace/project/tenant, execution ID or request ID, connection ID, Gmail account identity, operation name, and exact returned error/status.
Request a reproduction or preserved application log for a failed attempt so the search can be narrowed to a specific execution window.
Align the investigation window with the customer's last known successful send and first failed send to distinguish sudden breakage from an older latent issue.
Obtain the exact Gmail/API error text or OAuth refresh error from one failed execution before concluding consent was revoked.
If the eventual error shows revoked consent or insufficient scope, reconnect the intended Google account with the required scopes.
Verify that the reconnected account is the same intended sender identity before retrying.
Look for one failed provider response with HTTP status/error body before treating this as a provider outage.
Compare the affected tenant's Gmail sends with at least one unaffected tenant or account once telemetry is available to determine isolation.
If a provider rate/error response is eventually confirmed, monitor and back off rather than retry blindly.
